title: Self-Paced Module: Java Threads and Concurrency Tools

lessons.title: One Terminal, Many Dispatchers: What a Thread Is, and Its Life from start() to join()

objectives.cognitive: Explain what a thread is, how it differs from a process, and name the states a thread goes through from NEW to TERMINATED.
objectives.affective: Value other people's time by letting independent work happen together instead of making everyone wait in one line.
objectives.psychomotor: Write DispatchThread and StateWatcher, start them with start(), wait with join(), and show that a finished thread cannot be started again.

blocks.markdown:
**Where we left off:** your folder should already have `Vehicle.java`, `Jeepney.java`, `Tricycle.java`, `Bus.java`, `OverloadException.java`, `InvalidDistanceException.java`, and `VehicleNotFoundException.java`. Save a copy of `Main.java` as `Main_week15.txt`.

**The problem this week fixes:** every program so far does **one thing at a time**. If it waits for a slow job, everything else waits too. Java can do many things at once with **threads**.

**No internet needed.** Keep every class in its own file, all in one folder. Compile with `javac *.java`, run with `java Main`. Threads finish at different times, so every program this week prints its results **after** the threads finish, in a fixed order. The output is the same on every computer, even a slow one.

A **process** is a program that is running, with its own memory. A **thread** is one line of work **inside** a process. Every Java program starts with one thread, called `main`. Your program can start more threads; they run **at the same time** and **share** the process's memory. Threads of the same process can see the same objects; two different processes cannot.

The **terminal** is the process: one building, one logbook, one set of vehicles. The **dispatchers** are the threads. With one dispatcher (`main`), every job waits for the one before it. With three, one can load passengers, one can collect fares, one can call the next jeepney, all in the same terminal. The risk: two dispatchers writing in the same line of the logbook at once. So this week, **each thread uses only its own data**.

rows: a whole program that is running
one line of work inside a process
has its own; other processes cannot see it
shares the process's memory with its sibling threads
the whole terminal and its logbook
one dispatcher working in that terminal
main is the first; start() makes more

blocks.instruction: Make a new file `DispatchThread.java` and replace `Main.java`. The thread's job: collect 5 trips of fares, 0.1 second per trip. To make your own worker, write a class that **extends Thread** and **overrides** `run()`; call `start()`, never `run()` yourself; `join()` makes the caller wait until the thread is finished.
blocks.expectedOutput:
main() runs on thread: main
Before start(): NEW
After join(): TERMINATED
NXA 123 ran on thread: NXA 123
Collected after 5 trips: P75.0
blocks.checkYourself: (1) Change the 5 in `new DispatchThread(jeep, 5)` to 10 and predict the collected amount. (P150.0, because each trip adds P15.00; the printed text still says 5 trips, so fix that string.) (2) Why must `t.join()` be inside `try` and `catch (InterruptedException e)`? (`join()` and `sleep()` can throw this **checked** exception, as in Week 13.)

guided.discussion:
- Look at line 3. `Thread.currentThread().getName()` asks Java, "Which thread is running this line?" It answers main. Every Java program starts with one thread called main.
- Look at line 1 of DispatchThread.java. `public class DispatchThread extends Thread` is our own worker class. As you remember from Week 12, extends means the child gets everything the parent has, so a DispatchThread can do everything a Thread can.
- Look at line 8 of DispatchThread.java. `super(vehicle.getPlateNumber());` passes the plate up to Thread as the thread's name. As you remember from Week 12, super(...) calls the parent's constructor.
- Look at line 14 of DispatchThread.java. `public void run()` is the job the thread does. It overrides Thread's own run(). Line 17 adds one fare per trip with `vehicle.quoteFare(5)` from Vehicle.java, and line 19, `Thread.sleep(100)`, makes each trip take 0.1 second.
- Look at line 5. `new DispatchThread(jeep, 5)` makes a worker for the jeepney with 5 trips. This is the line the guided example changes.
- Look at line 7. `t.getState()` says NEW: the thread exists, but it has not started.
- Look at line 8. `t.start();` begins a new thread, and that new thread runs run().
- Look at line 10. `t.join();` makes main wait until the worker is finished. It sits inside a try, because join() can throw InterruptedException. As you remember from Week 13, a checked exception must be caught or declared.
- Look at line 14. After join(), the state is TERMINATED: run() has ended.
- Look at line 16. `t.getCollected()` is read only after join(), so the total is complete: 5 trips x P15.00 = P75.0.
guided.instruction: Now we make the jeepney run three trips. Change line 5 to the first line below, and line 16 to the second line. Then run. You should get this result.
guided.code:
DispatchThread t = new DispatchThread(jeep, 3);
        System.out.println("Collected after 3 trips: P" + t.getCollected());
guided.expectedOutput:
main() runs on thread: main
Before start(): NEW
After join(): TERMINATED
NXA 123 ran on thread: NXA 123
Collected after 3 trips: P45.0

solution.note: Each trip adds P15.00, the jeepney's fare for 5 km (Jeepney.java), so 4 trips collect P60.0. main reads the total only after join(), so it is complete.

blocks.markdown: **Look closely:** the thread is `NEW` before `start()` and `TERMINATED` after its `run()` ended. It was named by the plate number: `super(...)` passes the name up to `Thread`, just as `Jeepney`'s constructor passes values up to `Vehicle` in Week 12.

rows: The Thread object exists; start() was not called yet.
Started: running, or waiting its turn on the processor.
Paused for a set time, e.g. inside Thread.sleep(100).
Paused with no time limit, e.g. join() or await() with no wait time.
The run() method has finished. It cannot be started again.

blocks.instruction: Make a new file `StateWatcher.java` and replace `Main.java`. Watch one thread go through its life: NEW, running, sleeping, TERMINATED. Then try to start it a second time.
blocks.expectedOutput:
Before start(): NEW, alive? false
Inside run(): RUNNABLE
After join(): TERMINATED, alive? false
Start it again? Not allowed: a thread runs only once.
blocks.checkYourself: In `StateWatcher`, change `sleep(200)` to `sleep(2000)` and run. Predict the output. (**The same**, only 2 seconds slower: `join()` waits for the sleep to end.) Change it back.

guided.discussion:
- Look at line 1 of StateWatcher.java. `public class StateWatcher extends Thread` is another worker, like DispatchThread in Step 1.
- Look at line 5 of StateWatcher.java. `super(name);` gives the thread its name, TRC 456. As you remember from Week 12, super(...) calls the parent's constructor.
- Look at line 10 of StateWatcher.java. `seenInside = getState().toString();` The thread looks at its own state while it runs: RUNNABLE. getState() is a method of Thread. This is the line the guided example changes.
- Look at line 12 of StateWatcher.java. `Thread.sleep(200);` pauses the thread for 0.2 second. While it sleeps, its state is TIMED_WAITING. sleep() can throw InterruptedException, so it sits in a try. As you remember from Week 13, a checked exception must be caught or declared.
- Look at line 4. `w.getState()` says NEW, and `w.isAlive()` says false: the thread exists, but it has not started.
- Look at line 6. `w.start();` begins the new thread. It runs run() from StateWatcher.java.
- Look at line 8. `w.join();` makes main wait until run() ends, sleep and all.
- Look at line 13. `w.getState()` is now TERMINATED, and `w.isAlive()` is false again.
- Look at line 16. `w.start();` tries to start the same thread again. Java throws IllegalThreadStateException, which line 17 catches. A thread runs only once; to do the job again, make a new thread.
guided.instruction: Now the thread also checks that it is alive while it runs. Replace line 10 of StateWatcher.java with this line. Then run. You should get this result.
guided.expectedOutput:
Before start(): NEW, alive? false
Inside run(): RUNNABLE, alive? true
After join(): TERMINATED, alive? false
Start it again? Not allowed: a thread runs only once.

activity.instruction: Now do it on your own. Change the same line so the thread reports which thread is running it, with `Thread.currentThread().getName()`, in place of the alive check.
activity.expectedOutput:
Before start(): NEW, alive? false
Inside run(): RUNNABLE, on thread TRC 456
After join(): TERMINATED, alive? false
Start it again? Not allowed: a thread runs only once.

solution.lines:
StateWatcher.java, line 10 — the name of the thread running run():
        seenInside = getState() + ", on thread " + Thread.currentThread().getName();
solution.note: run() is running on the new thread, and its name is TRC 456 (given by super(name) at line 5). Thread.currentThread() gives the thread that runs this line.

blocks.markdown: **Look closely:** `isAlive()` is true only between `start()` and the end of `run()`. A finished thread cannot be started again: make a **new** thread object for each run (Error Guide, IllegalThreadStateException).

lessons.title: Start, Never Run: Many Dispatchers at the Same Time

objectives.cognitive: Explain why a program must call start() and not run(), and why main joins every thread before it reads the results.
objectives.affective: Value other people's time by letting independent work happen together instead of making everyone wait in one line.
objectives.psychomotor: Show the difference between start() and run(); start three threads, join them, and print the results in a fixed order.

blocks.markdown: **Yesterday** you made one thread, started it and waited for it. **Today:** the most common mistake (calling `run()` instead of `start()`), then three workers running **at the same time**.

- Look at line 7. `wrong.run();` is only an ordinary method call. No new thread starts, so main does the whole job itself. This is the line the guided example changes.
- Look at line 8. `wrong.getRanOn()` gives main, because main ran the job. getRanOn() is at line 27 of DispatchThread.java, and line 15 of that file saves the name of the thread that ran it.
- Look at line 11. `right.start();` starts a real new thread, named BUS 789.
- Look at line 13. `right.join();` waits for that thread to finish before line 17 prints.
- Look at line 17. `right.getRanOn()` gives BUS 789, the new thread's own name.

- Look at line 6. `List<DispatchThread> crew = new ArrayList<>();` As you remember from Week 14, a List grows as we add to it. Here it holds three workers.
- Look at line 7. `new DispatchThread(new Jeepney("NXA 123", "Mang Ramon", "Monumento-Divisoria"), 5)` gives the jeepney's worker 5 trips. Lines 8 and 9 do the same for the tricycle and the bus. The guided example changes the 5 on these three lines.

lessons.title: Job Orders, Roll Calls and Convoys: Runnable, CountDownLatch, and CyclicBarrier

objectives.cognitive: Describe what a Runnable is, how a CountDownLatch makes one thread wait for several others, and how a CyclicBarrier makes a group wait for each other again and again.
objectives.affective: Show responsibility by making sure every job reports back, even when something goes wrong.
objectives.psychomotor: Write a Runnable job and give it to a Thread; write ReadyReport and use a CountDownLatch so main waits for four reports; write ConvoyLeg with a CyclicBarrier used at two stops.

blocks.markdown: An **interface**: a promise that a class has certain methods. This one has just one, `void run()`. A class that **implements Runnable** describes **a job**. To get it done, hand the job to a `Thread`: `new Thread(job, "name")`. This is the usual way, because the job class can still extend another class, but a class can extend only one parent, and `Thread` would use it up.

`extends Thread` is like hiring a person **who comes with one job fixed to them**. `Runnable` is writing the job on a **work order** ("load these groups of passengers") and giving it to any available worker. The worker is the `Thread`, the order is the `Runnable`.

rows: a job class with run(), then new Thread(job)
Can the class extend another class?

blocks.instruction: Make `BoardingTask.java`, then replace `Main.java`. It uses Week 13's `board()` and `OverloadException`: each job catches its **own** exception.
blocks.expectedOutput:
Jeep loader: all boarded
Trike loader: stopped: TRC 456 is full! Capacity 4, but 5 tried to ride.
NXA 123 | Driver: Mang Ramon | Passengers: 19/20
TRC 456 | Driver: Kuya Ben | Passengers: 4/4
blocks.checkYourself: Change the jeepney's groups to `{5, 8, 8}` and run. Predict the first line. (`Jeep loader: stopped: NXA 123 is full! Capacity 20, but 21 tried to ride.` and the jeepney then shows 13/20, because the last group was refused.) Change it back.

guided.discussion:
- Look at line 1 of BoardingTask.java. `public class BoardingTask implements Runnable` says BoardingTask is a job, not a thread. Runnable is an interface with one method, run().
- Look at line 15 of BoardingTask.java. `vehicle.board(g);` is board() from Vehicle.java. As you remember from Week 13, board() throws our own OverloadException when too many riders try to board.
- Look at line 19 of BoardingTask.java. `catch (OverloadException e)` The job catches its own problem and saves it in result. It does not stop the other job.
- Look at line 6. `new int[] {5, 8, 6}` are the jeepney's groups: 5 + 8 + 6 = 19, and it has 20 seats.
- Look at line 7. `new int[] {2, 2, 1}` are the tricycle's groups. After 2 + 2 = 4, the last group of 1 would make 5 on a 4-seat tricycle, so board() refuses it. This is the line the guided example changes.
- Look at line 9. `new Thread(jeepJob, "Jeep loader")` hands the job to a Thread and gives the thread a name.
- Look at line 19. `jeepJob.getResult()` is read only after both joins, on lines 14 and 15.
- Look at line 21. `jeep.showInfo()` comes from Vehicle.java. It shows 19/20 for the jeepney; line 22 shows 4/4 for the tricycle.
guided.instruction: Now the tricycle takes smaller groups. Replace line 7 with this line. Then run. You should get this result.
guided.code: BoardingTask trikeJob = new BoardingTask(trike, new int[] {1, 1, 1});
guided.expectedOutput:
Jeep loader: all boarded
Trike loader: all boarded
NXA 123 | Driver: Mang Ramon | Passengers: 19/20
TRC 456 | Driver: Kuya Ben | Passengers: 3/4

solution.lines:
Main.java, line 7 — groups of 2, 1 and 1:
        BoardingTask trikeJob = new BoardingTask(trike, new int[] {2, 1, 1});
solution.note: board() refuses only when the riders would be MORE than the seats. 2 + 1 + 1 = 4 is not more than 4, so every group boards and the tricycle shows 4/4.

blocks.markdown: **Look closely:** the trike's job stopped when 5 people tried to ride a 4-seat tricycle (Week 13's `OverloadException`), but the jeepney's job was not affected. A job that catches its own problems cannot hurt the others.

Starts with a number, such as 4. Each worker calls `countDown()` when it is done, which lowers the number by 1. A thread that calls `await()` **waits until the number is 0**, then goes on. A latch is **one-shot**: once at 0, it cannot be reset.

The dispatcher says, "We leave when **4** vehicles report ready." Each driver radios in when ready. The dispatcher keeps a tally: 4, 3, 2, 1, 0. At 0 she blows the whistle. It does not matter **who** reports first, only that all 4 have.

blocks.instruction: Make `ReadyReport.java`, then replace `Main.java`. The vehicles take different times to get ready: 400, 100, 300, and 200 milliseconds.
blocks.expectedOutput:
Dispatcher waits. Reports still needed: 4
NXA 123 reports: ready
TRC 456 reports: ready
BUS 789 reports: ready
NYB 321 reports: ready
Reports still needed: 0
All vehicles ready. Dispatch begins!
blocks.checkYourself: Change `new CountDownLatch(4)` to `(5)` and run. Only 4 jobs call `countDown()`, so the count stops at 1 and the program **never ends**. Press Ctrl+C to stop it, then change it back.

guided.discussion:
- Look at line 7. `new CountDownLatch(4)` starts the count at 4: main will wait for 4 reports. The guided example changes this number.
- Look at line 9. `reports.add(new ReadyReport("NXA 123", 400, latch));` Lines 9 to 12 put four jobs in a List, each with its own time to get ready: 400, 100, 300 and 200 ms. All four share the same latch.
- Look at line 16. `new Thread(r).start();` hands each ReadyReport job to a new thread, as in Step 5.
- Look at line 19 of ReadyReport.java. `status = "ready";` The job saves its own result. It does not print, because the threads finish at different times and their prints could come in any order.
- Look at line 23 of ReadyReport.java. `latch.countDown();` lowers the count by 1. It sits in finally, so the count goes down even if the job fails. As you remember from Week 13, finally always runs.
- Look at line 19. `latch.await();` main stops here until the count reaches 0.
- Look at line 24. `r.getStatus()` is read after await(), in the list's order, so the output never changes.
- Look at line 26. `latch.getCount()` is now 0.

blocks.markdown: **Read it carefully:** the vehicles get ready in order of **speed** (TRC 100 ms first, NXA 400 ms last), not the order the threads were started. The jobs do not print; main prints every report after `await()`, in the list's order, so the output is the same every time. `countDown()` sits in `finally` (Week 13) so the count goes down even if something goes wrong in the job. Without it, `await()` could wait forever.

blocks.markdown: A `CyclicBarrier(3)` makes a group of **3** threads wait at a meeting point. Each calls `await()`. When the **3rd** arrives, all three are released together, and the barrier is **ready to use again**. `await()` gives back a number: **0 for the last thread to arrive**. Difference from a latch: here the **workers wait for each other**, and the barrier can be reused.
Three jeepneys travel as a **convoy**. At every stop they wait for each other, and leave only when all three have arrived. At the next stop they wait for each other again. One barrier, reused.

blocks.instruction: Make `ConvoyLeg.java`, then replace `Main.java`. It also needs `BrokenBarrierException`, a checked exception that `await()` can throw.
blocks.expectedOutput:

NYB 321 reached Recto

- Look at line 7. `new CyclicBarrier(3)` is a meeting point for 3 threads. The guided example changes this number.
- Look at line 9. `legs.add(new ConvoyLeg("NXA 123", 300, barrier));` Lines 9 to 11 put three convoy jobs in a List. All three share the same barrier.
- Look at line 15. `convoy.add(new Thread(leg));` gives each job its own thread, as in Step 5.
- Look at line 18 of ConvoyLeg.java. `Thread.sleep(delayMs);` is the drive to the stop: 300, 100 or 200 ms.
- Look at line 19 of ConvoyLeg.java. `barrier.await()` makes the vehicle wait until all 3 have arrived. It gives back 0 to the last one to arrive.
- Look at line 21 of ConvoyLeg.java. `System.out.println("-- All here at " + stop + ". The convoy moves on together!");` Only the last to arrive prints it, so it prints once for each stop.
- Look at line 30 of ConvoyLeg.java. `driveTo("Recto");` uses the same barrier again. That is the cyclic part: the barrier is ready again after every meeting.
- Look at line 17 of ConvoyLeg.java. `throws InterruptedException, BrokenBarrierException` As you remember from Week 13, throws passes checked exceptions to the caller. run() catches both at line 31.
- Look at line 28. `leg.getLastStop()` is read after every join, in the list's order, so the output never changes.

lessons.title: Loading Bays: Sharing Limited Places with Semaphore

objectives.cognitive: Explain how a Semaphore uses permits with acquire() and release(), and choose between CountDownLatch, CyclicBarrier, and Semaphore for a given situation.
objectives.affective: Practice fairness by letting limited resources, such as loading bays, be shared in turn.
objectives.psychomotor: Write LoadingBay with a Semaphore of two permits, and BayBoarding, which always gives its bay back even when a vehicle is refused.

blocks.markdown: A `Semaphore(2)` holds **2 permits**. `acquire()` takes one permit, or **waits** if none is left. `release()` gives one back. So at most 2 threads are in the protected part at once. `availablePermits()` tells how many are free. Put `release()` in `finally` so a permit is never lost.
The terminal has **2 loading bays**. A vehicle that arrives takes a bay if one is free; otherwise it waits in line. When a vehicle leaves, it frees its bay for the next one. The permits are the bays.

guided.discussion:
- Look at line 7. `new Semaphore(2)` makes 2 permits, one for each loading bay. The guided example changes this number.
- Look at line 8. `bays.availablePermits()` tells how many bays are free: 2 at the start.
- Look at line 10. `jobs.add(new LoadingBay("NXA 123", 0, bays));` Lines 10 to 13 make four jobs from LoadingBay.java. They arrive 0, 100, 200 and 300 ms after the start, and all four share the same bays.
- Look at line 19 of LoadingBay.java. `bays.acquire();` takes a bay. If both bays are busy, the thread waits here. BUS 789 arrives at 200 ms, while NXA 123 and TRC 456 are still loading, so it waits.
- Look at line 21 of LoadingBay.java. `Thread.sleep(400);` Loading takes 0.4 second.
- Look at line 24 of LoadingBay.java. `bays.release();` gives the bay back. It sits in finally, so the bay always comes back. As you remember from Week 13, finally always runs.
- Look at line 30. `job.getResult()` is read after every join, in the list's order. The vehicles load in turns, but the output never changes.
- Look at line 32. `bays.availablePermits()` is 2 again: every bay came back.

Main.java, line 7 — three bays:
        Semaphore bays = new Semaphore(3);                 // 3 bays
solution.note: A Semaphore(3) holds 3 permits, so 3 vehicles can load at once. Every acquire() is matched by a release() in finally, so all 3 bays are free again at the end.

blocks.markdown: **What happens inside** (not printed, because the order could change on a slow computer): NXA 123 (0 ms) and TRC 456 (100 ms) take the 2 bays. BUS 789 (200 ms) and NYB 321 (300 ms) find **Free bays: 0**, so they wait at `acquire()`. When NXA 123 leaves (400 ms), BUS 789 takes its bay. When TRC 456 leaves (500 ms), NYB 321 takes that one. At no time are more than 2 vehicles loading.

**PART F — A bay that always comes back.** In real terminals, some vehicles are turned away: too many riders, or a problem with the trip. If a vehicle takes a bay and is refused, the bay must still be given back, or the vehicles behind it wait forever. `release()` in `finally` (Week 13) makes sure every permit returns.

rows.means: The same Thread object had start() called twice. A thread can run only once.

rows.see: ran on thread: main when you expected the worker's name

rows.see: Exception in thread "Bad trip" InvalidDistanceException: ... and the program carries on

performanceTask.title: Performance Task: Make Your Program Do Many Things at Once
performanceTask.markdown:
Open your own program from your Four Pillars Performance Task (your sari-sari store, pets, gadgets, school personnel, or shapes theme). Give it **helpers that work at the same time**, and make them wait for each other the right way. Start on Thursday after the Thursday exit slip; finish and present on Friday.

**Reuse this week's code.** Your helper class works like `BoardingTask` (Step 5) or `DispatchThread` (Step 1); the latch like Step 6; the barrier like Step 7; the semaphore like Step 8. The example shows only the latch: **you must add a second tool.**

**Example (sari-sari store, two cashiers):**

- Ana rang up Bread P12
- Ben rang up Soap P18
- Ana rang up Rice P55
- Ben rang up Coffee P9
- Ana's total: P67 / Ben's total: P27 / Store total: P94

**Testing tip:** run your program at least four ways: (1) normally; (2) three times in a row: the totals must be identical; (3) change one sleep time: the order of messages changes, but the totals do not; (4) give one helper bad data: it must be caught and the others must still finish. No run may end in `Exception in thread "main"`, and none may hang.

**Plan before you type** (show your teacher): for each helper, write its name, whether it is a Thread or a Runnable, its job, its own data, and which tool joins it in, and why.
steps: In Projects, click **Personal performance-task project**. Your own program opens.
On paper, for each helper write its name, whether it is a Thread or a Runnable, its job, its own data, and which tool waits for it, and why. Show your teacher.
Add a helper class file. Copy **Step 5 · BoardingTask.java** (Runnable) or **Step 1 · DispatchThread.java** (Thread), paste it, and change it for your theme. Give each helper a name that is printed.
In `main`, make at least 3 helpers and begin each with `start()`, never `run()`, like **Step 3 · Main.java**. Each helper changes only its own data.
Use `Thread.sleep()` to show that work takes time, and handle every `InterruptedException`.
Add a `CountDownLatch`: `countDown()` in `finally` inside each helper, and `await()` in `main`, like **Step 6 · ReadyReport.java**. **Sample code · Cashier.java** shows the store example.
Add a second tool that fits your story: a `Semaphore`, like **Step 8 · LoadingBay.java**, or a `CyclicBarrier`, like **Step 7 · ConvoyLeg.java**.
Print the results after everyone has finished, in a fixed order, like **Step 4 · Main.java**.
Give one helper bad data and catch it inside its `run()`. The other helpers must still finish.
Test four ways: normally; three times in a row (same totals); with one sleep time changed (order changes, totals do not); with bad data in one helper. No run may crash or hang.
Add a comment on each part, for example `// LATCH: store opens when both cashiers finish`.
Tick each item in the **Performance task checklist**, then click **Submit this version**.
checklist: At least 3 helper objects from your theme, each doing its own job on its own thread
Helpers built with extends Thread or implements Runnable; each has a name that is printed
Each thread changes only its own data, no shared variable
A CountDownLatch, with countDown() in finally, and await() in main
A second tool: Semaphore or CyclicBarrier, with a story that fits your theme
Thread.sleep() shows work takes time; every InterruptedException is handled
Results are printed after everyone has finished, in a fixed order
Bad data in one helper is caught inside its run(); the others still finish
A comment on each part, e.g. // LATCH: store opens when both cashiers finish
presentationOutline: Introduce your theme and your helpers. (30 sec)
Run it and show the output. (1 min)
Prove it live: run it again; change a sleep; break it on purpose. (2 min)
Point to the code for a thread, the latch, and the second tool. (1 min)
questionsToPrepare: What does your latch count? What if the number is too big?
Why print the totals after the threads finish?
What could go wrong if two threads changed one variable?

rubric.criterion: Threads: 3+ helpers started with start(); named; finish before results are shown
Design: Thread or Runnable used correctly; each thread keeps its own data
Tools: latch used correctly; a second tool that fits the story
Results: same correct totals on every run, in a fixed order
Errors: InterruptedException and bad data handled; no crash, no hang
Presentation and Q&A: proves each part live; explains choices with own code
